results.name: shared_contained_digit_tens
results.description: In 2-4 example sets where every example contains a common digit d, among non-example targets more than 5 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets whose tens digit is such a d minus other such targets; observed above the null means people use 'contains digit d' rules more than the model, below means the model over-weights those rules.
results.code:
# name: shared_contained_digit_tens
# description: In 2-4 example sets where every example contains a common digit d, among non-example targets more than 5 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets whose tens digit is such a d minus other such targets; observed above the null means people use 'contains digit d' rules more than the model, below means the model over-weights those rules.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    Ei = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1).astype(int)
    valid = Ei >= 0
    common = np.ones((len(t), 10), dtype=bool)
    for d in range(10):
        has = (np.mod(Ei, 10) == d) | ((Ei // 10) % 10 == d) & (Ei >= 10) | (Ei == 100) & (d in (0, 1))
        common[:, d] = np.all(has | ~valid, axis=1)
    ti = t.astype(int)
    tens = np.where(ti >= 10, (ti // 10) % 10, -1)
    hit = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for d in range(10):
        hit |= common[:, d] & (tens == d)
    m = (~is_ex) & (n >= 2) & (~share_fd) & (dist > 5) & common.any(axis=1)
    return rate(m & hit) - rate(m & (~hit))

results.name: single_example_parity_match
results.description: For single-example sets, among non-example targets more than 3 from the example and not sharing its final digit, yes-rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed above the null means people generalize a lone example's parity (odd/even rule) more than the model, below means the model over-weights parity rules for one example.
results.code:
# name: single_example_parity_match
# description: For single-example sets, among non-example targets more than 3 from the example and not sharing its final digit, yes-rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed above the null means people generalize a lone example's parity (odd/even rule) more than the model, below means the model over-weights parity rules for one example.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    same_par = np.mod(np.nan_to_num(E[:, 0]), 2) == np.mod(t, 2)
    m = (~is_ex) & (n == 1) & (~share_fd) & (dist > 3)
    return rate(m & same_par) - rate(m & (~same_par))

results.name: single_example_near_gradient
results.description: For single-example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets 1-3 from the example minus targets 4-10 from it; observed above the null means people's generalization from a lone example falls off within the first few numbers faster than the fitted width prior implies, below means the model's near falloff is too steep.

    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)

results.name: two_example_gap_fill
results.description: In 2-example sets whose examples are 4-30 apart, among non-example targets sharing no final digit with an example and within half the gap of the nearest example, yes-rate for targets strictly between the examples minus those outside them; observed above the null means people interpolate between two close examples more (vs extrapolating) than the model's interval posterior, below means less.
results.code:
# name: two_example_gap_fill
# description: In 2-example sets whose examples are 4-30 apart, among non-example targets sharing no final digit with an example and within half the gap of the nearest example, yes-rate for targets strictly between the examples minus those outside them; observed above the null means people interpolate between two close examples more (vs extrapolating) than the model's interval posterior, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    lo = np.nanmin(E, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    gap = hi - lo
    m = (~is_ex) & (n == 2) & (gap >= 4) & (gap <= 30) & (~share_fd) & (dist <= gap / 2.0)
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    return rate(m & inside) - rate(m & (~inside))

results.name: same_digit_distance_gradient
results.description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets sharing a final digit with some example, yes-rate for those within 10 of the nearest example minus those more than 30 from every example; the model's final-digit rules are flat in magnitude, so observed above the null means people's digit-rule generalization decays with distance more than the model predicts (below means less).

# description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets sharing a final digit with some example, yes-rate for those within 10 of the nearest example minus those more than 30 from every example; the model's final-digit rules are flat in magnitude, so observed above the null means people's digit-rule generalization decays with distance more than the model predicts (below means less).
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)

        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    m = (~is_ex) & (n >= 2) & share_fd

results.name: repdigit_target_generalization
results.description: In sets containing a repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate for non-example repdigit targets sharing no final digit with any example minus other non-example targets sharing no final digit and more than 3 from every example; observed above the null means people use a 'same two digits' rule the model lacks, below means they avoid those targets more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: repdigit_target_generalization
# description: In sets containing a repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate for non-example repdigit targets sharing no final digit with any example minus other non-example targets sharing no final digit and more than 3 from every example; observed above the null means people use a 'same two digits' rule the model lacks, below means they avoid those targets more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    rep_ex = np.any((E >= 11) & (np.mod(E, 11) == 0), axis=1)
    rep_t = (t >= 11) & (np.mod(t, 11) == 0)
    m = (~is_ex) & rep_ex & (~share_fd)
    return rate(m & rep_t) - rate(m & (~rep_t) & (dist > 3))

results.name: far_target_magnitude_asymmetry
results.description: In all sets, among non-example targets more than 15 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for small targets (<=30) minus large targets (>=70); observed above the null means people favour small numbers as far generalizations more than the model's compressed number line predicts, below means the model over-produces the small-number bias.
